blocks.x: Recently, I began taunting colleagues with an idea. I say “taunting” because the idea was not really an idea at all. It was not even a proper sentence. It was just a couple of words: two kids. The magazine professional in your life will be reading this and shaking their head. In our business, you’re supposed to have a new take. You’re supposed to be able to make the room see the proposed story with a few well-turned phrases and a detailed plan. You’re not supposed to simply point to your two young progeny and say: There they are, isn’t this crazy?

I did intend to get around to the actual take at some point. Ideally, before arriving at the second paragraph of this thing. But having two kids does stuff to you. An idea lodges in your brain, but the thought never finishes. It is borne away in a flood of tears, a chronic bad back, a kitchen so radically destroyed it takes an hour and 15 minutes to restore.
There they are, though. Two boys: Knox and Cy. Isn’t this crazy?

When my wife (whom I will try to mention sparingly here, as per a long-standing agreement between us) was pregnant with Cy, our second, I began to receive the clichés from other parents, like a ritual hazing. You’re going from zone defense to man-to-man. Or a throw-pillow-style one that I actually liked: You think you can’t love the second one as much as you love the first, but then your heart just expands. Lovely thought. My actual experience was a little different. When Cy arrived, shouldering his way into the world, it felt like coming home and finding the furniture rearranged. Same house, but also not. Everything in a slightly new place.

We were always two-kid people, enough so to go back to the shadow world of IVF for a second time. I can’t remember when the sliver of doubt about the prospect of another one crept in for me. Even acknowledging the doubt feels illicit now, with Cy walking around. (It’s like a prance: on his toes, almost getting air with each step, always on his way somewhere.) But it did happen. This feeling of impending doom: What have I done to what remains of my life? Part of it was that Knox was so captivating to me: a drummer, a joy machine, a professional enthusiast. Part of it was that I was already so tired and couldn’t figure out what being more tired than that would even mean. Part of it was a hunch that turned out to be true: We were losing something real and giant in terms of our freedom, our respective abilities to live big selfish lives.

When Cy was born, he had a routine complication: transient tachypnea of the newborn, or TTN. Fluid in the lungs. Basically, in the hours after his birth he could barely breathe. There was a moment of focused panic in the delivery room, and then the wheeled cart that took him to the NICU. I sat in a chair next to him, next to the little plastic box they put the babies into, and watched the monitor they’d hooked him up to showing his oxygen levels. You think you can’t love the second one as much as you love the first, but then your heart just expands.

blocks.x: Here is my cliché, for what little it’s worth: A parent with one child has more in common with a childless person than they have with a parent of two. I am reluctant by nature to give other parents advice, to try to generalize my own personal experience. But I had one and now I have two, and it is simply not the same. One feels hard precisely because of how much connection remains, tantalizingly, with your old life: your old hobbies, your old friends, your old functioning brain. With one, you even get to visit this old life from time to time, while your partner or some kindly person at day care takes their turn getting annihilated. With two, that old life is so completely gone it’s like it never even happened. It is a planet you cannot return to.
(With three, I’m told you simply give up. I myself will never find out.)

I remember the day we brought Cy home, the sweet way that Knox edged his face over the car seat to greet, for the first time, this stranger to whom he was now forever bound—and then the way he walked away, distracted by a mote of dust on a sunbeam and the possibility of something fun in another room. No walking away for us. That night, I gave Knox a bath. He got upset and started crying. It took me more than a moment, while trying to comfort my older son, to realize that I, in fact, heard two children crying—Cy, in the other room, was Dopplering his way into the conversation. There was nowhere to hide, no other party to hand the problem off to. This was day one.

blocks.x: There is the ego death of becoming a parent (my child is now the most important thing in my life), and then there is the ego death of becoming the parent of two (I have not had a moment or thought of my own since dawn). The sheer amount of hours you spend looking after them in these first few years. I sometimes think about an energetic and physically fit single friend of mine, a film director, who has become a surrogate uncle to my kids. He might be their favorite person in the world. And vice versa. They hang out all the time; he comes way out of his way to do it. If he and I were to actually switch lives, even for a day, he would die. He wouldn’t make it.

There is a level of boredom and hysteria that you learn to just kind of float through. Episodes that in your old life would be the most intense thing that happened to you in a month, or a year. Your child on the sidewalk, screaming, grinding his face angrily into a pile of dirt and concrete while strangers walk by with pity or disgust in their eyes. Maybe you have to physically restrain the little fellow from running into traffic. There is a quality of patience you attain: It feels like infinite acceptance and being on fire at the same time. And then you forget, because not forgetting would be unbearable.

Why did we do this? It’s a funny question. You’d expect me to have an answer. I don’t, exactly. Did we do it for them, so that they would have each other, either now or later, when we’re dying or dead? Did our egos demand a second monument? I genuinely can’t say. The absence in my life before becoming a parent was two-kid-shaped, is the best way I can put it.

What I did not know is that one kid is less than half of two kids. That a second kid would not amount to one extra tantrum per day, or one additional cold per month, because, as another father of two explained to me, adding kids to a family is geometry, not arithmetic. A four-person family contains six relationships, six vectors for squabbling or sharing viruses. “When you add the other 11 kids in your two-year-old’s day care class to the equation,” he said, “10 vectors became 100.” Make sense to you? No? Me neither. Perfect.

So: One hundred times the chance, at any given moment, that one of them has a cold or a tantrum. One hundred times the chance that one of them takes off running, or falling, down the 57 stone steps that lead up to our home. One hundred times the laundry. One hundred times the chance of a child accelerating to full speed and launching the crown of their skull into a wall, or your abdomen.

The other day, I went out, leaving my wife with the two of them. As I headed for the door, I noted the grimace. It is an expression I have come to recognize, one I have mastered myself. Loving mutual appreciation and deep, seething resentment, papered over with a half-hearted smile, all in one weary look. And when that door closes, and you are on the other side of it from your children? I want all of you to have two kids, just to have this feeling. Walking out into the night with a song in your heart loud enough to drown out whatever is happening behind that door you just closed.

blocks.x: In the two and a half years before Cy arrived, I got to know Knox pretty well. It is an amazing thing, just to watch your kid be your kid every day. For most of his life, we’ve been locking him in his room at night. He’d proved prone to wandering after dark, and our childproofing in certain spots, such as around the kitchen knives, was less than ideal. So I got a hook-and-eye latch and mounted it to the outside of the door, which sounds horrific but I swear we read in a book, the author and/or title of which now escapes me.

Then one day Knox expressed displeasure with the pull-up diaper he was forced, under this arrangement, to wear at night. I couldn’t argue with that. We went over the new rules: He could use the bathroom, just outside his bedroom, whenever it was called for. Then he would go straight back to his room. No laps around the house. Solemnly, he agreed. That night, I heard his door open and, in time, the toilet flush, and the small footsteps back to his room. Five minutes later, his door opened again, and the sequence repeated itself. And then again. Drunk with his own power, he spent about an hour traveling the four feet from his room to the bathroom and back, reveling in his newfound freedom.
Many days I find myself trying to explain to Knox or Cy the job of a brother: Protect each other at all costs, is what I try to reinforce. Be an ally to him, even against us. Especially against us.

At first, I assumed that Cy was basically just a smaller version of Knox. That he, too, in time, would do all the same Knox stuff. A new model of the same device. It took me longer than it should’ve to realize he was someone else entirely. The thing about the second one is that, in some ways, they never get your full attention. It’s one of the many injustices of being born second. Knox got bespoke parenting: special food, lovingly prepared. Hours of googling at the slightest disturbance in the force. Generous trips to the doctor. He flew on planes. Planes! Cy doesn’t even know what a plane is, hardly. No one—certainly not his parents—has bothered to tell him. Cy doesn’t get bespoke parenting. He gets hand-me-down parenting. A wave and a tolerant smile and a pair of pants that are either too big or too small but never exactly the right size.

And yet in my inattention a personality bloomed: sly, willful, deeply stubborn. Mischievous, above all else. At the restaurant last night, Cy berated our nice waiter with a yell that could be heard across the outdoor patio: “KETCHUP!”

The temptation one has, if you have a boisterous kid like Knox, is to assume the second one will be quieter: the artist, the poet, the sensitive one. The reality unveiling itself is quite different. Cy is even more boisterous. An athlete, even in his current state of one-and-a-half-year-old uncoordination. The first word I can remember him saying is ball. One day Knox will bully Cy with the blithe assurance of an older brother, as he does most days, and find himself thrown clear through a fucking wall.

I am one of two myself. I have a sister, younger by two years. I have some regrets about how I handled this situation. We’re very close now, but once, at dinner with her and our parents, I made a kind of passing joke about not realizing that I even had a sister until we were both in college. Everyone just sort of nodded, in solemn confirmation. Many days I find myself trying to explain to Knox or Cy the job of a brother: Protect each other at all costs, is what I try to reinforce. Be an ally to him, even against us. Especially against us.

Nothing can wound Cy like Knox’s cruelty—there is a kind of abject wail, a deep angry sound, that comes from Cy when Knox takes something out of his hand, or closes a door in his face. And nothing, as a parent, is more narcotic than the sound of them snapping into sync: giggling, tumbling on top of each other, yelling back and forth in ever greater hilarity. These are memories they will share with only each other—the texture of the wood floors in our house, the way dust and spiderwebs build up in the corners for our lack of attention to them. The way their mother looks in the first hour of the morning, contacts not yet in, glasses on. Only they will know what we have visited upon them.

A common experience of parenting is repeating something to your child, over and over again, with no real idea if it’s registering or getting through. These days the way I know it’s getting through is if I hear Knox say it to Cy. Take a deep breath, he tells his brother when he’s upset and can’t calm down. Be kind, when Cy tries to hit him or take something of his away. Stop it—an angry shout, here, not unlike one I’m sure I’ve directed at Knox a thousand times. And then I watch Cy watch Knox.

blocks.x: Friends of ours, one-kid people, recently moved to Paris for work, just because they wanted to. That makes sense, I thought. Having one kid is like adding a companion in the grand adventure of your life. Having two becomes the adventure itself. Even just the sheer logistics of moving two maniacs through this dangerous, indifferent, expensive world. It can overcome you.

They set the agenda, the two boys. But also: I like the agenda. I like the way it sharpens everything, the way everything in your life is compressed again, and again, until what remains is what is essential. There is no focus like the focus one has when one has 15 free minutes, or a three-day work trip. It’s a trade-off, it’s a magnifying glass, it’s a stopwatch. It’s a mirror: For one moment, amid the fog, there you are.

And I like the work of getting to know them both. My wife said that she’d recently realized that she had often looked for the two of us in Knox—What features of ours did he have? What personality traits?—and almost never in Cy. This was unfair, she decided: Knox ought to be allowed to be his own person, not just represent us.

In fact, one reason we had a second was to free Knox from the tractor beam of our interest. A tableau I’d sometimes witness before Cy was born: the two of us, maybe some friends or our parents, as many as five or six adults, all in a loose circle around Knox, just watching. We thought it’d probably be better for him in the long term if he wasn’t always the center of everything. A brutal but essential lesson. And for us, learning to love two in the same way we’d loved one? Also an essential lesson, and sometimes also brutal. Most days, especially when solo parenting, I feel one of two things—either completely empty and hollowed out for all the attention I’ve poured out for the two of them, or guilty, for having not paid enough attention at all.

Knox, at four, is just entering his lurch-away years—school and drum lessons and T-ball. Already, I have the experience of dropping him off somewhere, of closing a door, and for some small amount of time he and I live separate lives. Cy’s need for us is more urgent. Sometimes I feel some pain, perceiving it, because I know it won’t last. Another parenting cliché you get handed: Your job is to make yourself obsolete. I think of a mug that came in a fancy toy-subscription box we had for a while: “The days are long but the years are short.” At least, I think that’s what it said. The actual mug was inadvertently smashed by one of the four of us months ago, victim of the perpetual and ongoing chaos of our lives, which I am in no hurry to relinquish.

There is the ego death of becoming a parent (my child is now the most important thing in my life), and then there is the ego death of becoming the parent of two (I have not had a moment or thought of my own since dawn). A version of this story originally appeared in the October 2026 issue of GQ with the title “My Second Child Is Perfect. He Ruined My Life.”
